value.why: The generation plumbing is commodity: Gemini text and image endpoints, Veo for video, TTS for voiceover, Search grounding for the digest, all of it behind Cloud Functions and Cloud Tasks with Firestore for job state - a small team can stand up two or three of these in a month, and the page says its own build was substantially done with Gemini coding agents and Antigravity, which is a claim about speed of authoring, not about defensibility. What is not commodity is the per-vertical taste that makes each output acceptable - what a staged living room has to look like for a listing agent to send it, how a menu photo has to be lit - plus auth, billing, analytics and the trust required for a business to hand a workspace its brand. And the acquisition story the record actually claims as its accomplishment is founder-led outreach at $0 spend, which cannot be cloned at all: the moat named in the page is the team's ability to sell to SMBs, not the pipeline.

data_and_models.value: No model is trained and none is claimed to be. The system is an orchestration layer over vendor capabilities: Gemini APIs across text generation and analysis, image generation and editing, video, speech and Google Search-grounded intelligence, with Veo and gemini-tts named in the tag list as the specific generators. On the serving side it is Firebase Cloud Functions plus Cloud Tasks for asynchronous generation, Firestore and Cloud Storage for job state and produced assets, Secret Manager for credentials, Firebase hosting, auth, logging and analytics, with React and Node/Express at the edge. The authored content is notable for what it does not say: no model version is named for any of the five capability classes, no routing rule is given for which workflow calls which model, and no per-generation cost, latency or failure rate is published - which matters because the page itself explains that some operations are computationally intensive and asynchronous, so those three quantities are the product's real economic constraints.

how_it_works.value: Built 'AI-native from day one', beginning as workflow prototypes in Google AI Studio. The page credits Gemini-powered coding agents and Google Antigravity for architecture brainstorming, coding, testing, debugging and iteration, and Google Stitch for the frontend design process. In production the shape is an asynchronous architecture for AI workloads: Firebase Cloud Functions and Cloud Tasks orchestrate generation jobs, while Firestore and Cloud Storage hold job state and generated assets, on top of the authentication, logging and analytics that Firebase and Google Cloud provide. Model use is spread across capability classes rather than one endpoint - Gemini APIs for text generation and analysis, image generation and editing, video, speech, and Google Search-grounded intelligence - with Node/Express and React at the edges and the twenty-five-item Built With list also naming Veo, gemini-tts, Secret Manager and serverless. AI is also used internally: market analysis, customer targeting, UX development, debugging and documentation.

how_they_tested.value: Nothing is measured in the sense this catalog counts as measurement. There is no test suite, no eval, no accuracy, acceptance or rejection-rate figure, and no quality claim for any of the nine workflows - no statement, for instance, of how often a generated virtual-staged room or product video is acceptable to the business that asked for it. What the page offers instead is usage: 'early customer usage has been important in helping us make those decisions' between impressive-sounding and genuinely valuable features, which is product research rather than a test result, and 13 businesses as the population it was gathered from, unpublished per workflow. The one appearance of the word testing is in the description of how the code was written - Gemini-powered coding agents and Antigravity used for 'architecture brainstorming, coding, testing, debugging and iteration' - so the assertion is that testing happened, with no harness, count or result attached and no repository to read it from. The absence is load-bearing for a claim of this shape: the acceptance rate of a generated marketing image is the number a buyer of this product would need.

limits_they_disclosed.value: Three, and all three are stated as product restraint rather than technical failure. The first is 'avoiding the temptation to simply put powerful AI models behind generic prompt boxes' - owners want an outcome, so the workflows are organised around what the business is trying to accomplish, with most prompting and model complexity abstracted behind the experience. The second is workload heterogeneity: text, image, video and research jobs differ by orders of magnitude in cost, some completing quickly while others are computationally intensive and asynchronous, and the Cloud Tasks plus Firebase layer is what keeps that invisible to the user. The third is described as a continual judgement call between features that are technically impressive and features that create genuine value, with early customer usage cited as the thing that decided it.

what_breaks_first.value: Unit economics on the expensive workflows, then the quality question nobody measured. A $49/month plan is priced against a catalogue that includes Veo-class video generation and image editing for every customer; one realtor rendering a dozen listings a week can out-earn the subscription in inference on its own, and the page publishes no per-generation cost, latency or failure rate - while simultaneously admitting that some operations are computationally intensive and asynchronous, i.e. it knows exactly where the exposure is. Second: nine workflows means nine vendor surfaces, each with its own silent quality drift, and there is no acceptance metric for any of them, so a model version bump changes what a customer receives with nothing in the loop to notice. Third: '13 businesses using it' has no denominator - not paying, not retained, not per-workflow - so the traction claim that carries the record cannot be turned into a rate by a reader at all.

what_it_does.value: attainDesk turns common small-business needs into guided, business-specific AI workflows from one workspace: create social-media content; virtually stage real-estate listings; turn property images into video tours; create short promotional product videos; transform ordinary food photos into polished menu and marketing images; generate business logos; create professional headshots; generate branded meeting backgrounds; and a Daily Digest that surfaces relevant market developments, local business groups, events and opportunities. The named verticals are real estate, food, manufacturing, construction, education, clothing and professional services. The features differ and the goal is stated as one: help a small business understand its market, present itself professionally, reach customers and grow without needing a large specialist team.

what_it_is.value: An AI-native operations workspace for small businesses, where each business outcome - virtual staging a listing, turning food photos into menu images, a product video, a logo, a headshot, a Daily Digest of local opportunities - is its own guided workflow over an asynchronous Firebase Cloud Functions and Cloud Tasks generation pipeline, on the stated premise that owners should not have to learn AI to put it to work.

what_to_steal.value: Refuse the prompt box. The stated design principle - users describe a business outcome while model selection, prompting, context and iteration happen behind the scenes - is transferable to any vertical agent, and the async plumbing that makes it survivable is the second half: Cloud Functions plus Cloud Tasks so a two-second text job and a two-minute video job share one UI contract with Firestore holding job state. Then steal the honesty of the product framing itself: 'the best AI experience can sometimes feel like there is less AI, not more' is the line to put on a wall in any team shipping a model-backed workflow, and the Digest-that-found-the-first-customer loop is a template for pointing your own research surface at your own acquisition problem.

value.why: The visible surface is days of work - a React PWA with voice and camera input, an Express API on Cloud Run, Firestore, and a Gemini call that turns Spanish into an expression mathjs evaluates. The cost is everything they built so the money can be trusted: the parse-to-expression boundary, the invariant suite (167 tests, including 'never hand-repair a broken money JSON' and 'an agent never gives orders'), the accuracy agent that separates wrong from blind, and a defensive parser for a government HTML page that 503s non-browser clients and has no API. data_and_models.value: Receipt photographs, voice and typed Spanish queries, per-user purchase history and daily books in Firestore. Two model uses only, both non-arithmetic: natural-language parsing into a structured expression and receipt line transcription (gemini-3.5-flash). Every number is evaluated by mathjs in code. External data is SNIIM, the Mexican Ministry of Economy's market price system - 49 central markets, 222 products, no API - obtained by defensively parsing an ASP.NET HTML page with browser-like headers and pinning a real saved response as a regression test. how_it_works.value: React 19 PWA on the front, Node.js and Express on Cloud Run serving API and PWA from the same origin, Firestore for data, Gemini (gemini-3.5-flash) for natural-language parsing and receipt transcription, mathjs for arithmetic. The central decision is stated as the one the whole product rests on: the model never does arithmetic - Gemini turns language into a structured expression and code evaluates it, because 'a language model is not a calculator, and money does not tolerate a plausible answer'. The agents are five Cloud Run Jobs triggered by Cloud Scheduler: no laptop open, no session running, retries on failure, every run logged. Wholesale prices come from SNIIM, the Mexican Ministry of Economy's market price system - 49 central markets, 222 products, no API - so the backend parses the HTML of an ASP.NET page defensively and tests against a real saved response 'so we find out the day the government changes the page'. Jest, 167 tests.

how_they_tested.value: 167 Jest tests, named as including the invariants that matter: that a broken money JSON is never repaired by hand, that an agent never gives orders, that a receipt which does not balance cannot be saved. Separate from the unit suite, an accuracy agent scores twelve cases daily and distinguishes 'wrong' from 'no answer', so a Gemini overload day produced 10/10 with 2 unanswered rather than a false alarm. On the record's own evaluation of 30 cases the reported result is 0 errors with a 95% upper bound on the error rate of about 10%, and that bound reproduces exactly (1 - 0.05^(1/30) = 9.5%). Unit costs were read from usageMetadata and then cross-checked against the billing report's output-token line. No repository or CI link appears on the page, so the harness itself cannot be read; the figures it reports can.

limits_they_disclosed.value: Four problems are told as diagnoses, two of them as wrong diagnoses. The cold start: the price alert could only compare a user's own history, so it needed three purchases of the same product before it could say anything, and in production that read avisos_creados=0 day after day - 'not a hypothesis, a measurement' - which is what forced the fifth agent and the SNIIM integration. A government endpoint answering 503 to anything without browser headers, for data that is public and free by mandate. The receipts-coming-back-truncated bug, where the team assumed the model was running out of output budget, added finishReason logging to confirm it, and the data said STOP rather than MAX_TOKENS: the model was stopping on its own, mid-word, deterministically at temperature 0. And two money bugs: Costco prints the weight on the line above the item, so the model copied the line amount into the unit price field and 2.845 kg at $433.64 became $1,233 for a row that reads $433.64 - the backend summed by line amount and said it balanced while the screen recomputed and said it did not, two sources of truth for the same number, leaving a user with a disabled save button and no way out; then a discount living in the totals block below the subtotal that the model kept forgetting. Even the Spanish gave them away: the first market alert said 'papa esta mas barato', wrong gender, fixed by putting an article on all 28 products and rewriting the message around a verb, which carries none.

value.relation: same users, same language, opposite relationship to being wrong. Finova is a Spanish-language personal finance app that prices a gamified ledger off six live external feeds; it discloses no failure mode, publishes no evaluation and is held at `thin` for it. CALC is the answer to the same problem stated as a correctness contract - refuse to save unverifiable money, publish the confidence bound - which makes the pair the clearest illustration in the corpus that 'money app' is not an evidence class.

convergent instinct, different mechanism. AttainDesk's conclusion after a year of SMB support work was 'less AI, not more'; CALC removes the model from the arithmetic entirely. Both arrive at narrowing the model's authority by watching where it fails, and both are listed at the same Build with Gemini XPRIZE showcase.

two records where the model acts only behind a gate the code enforces - failing unit tests block a pull request there, a non-balancing receipt blocks a save here. ZeroDay's gate has no published result or denominator; CALC's gate ships with a test count, an eval set and a bound, which is why one publishes as a full record and the other's headline figure reads as a slogan.

the same 'never assert what you could not see' rule, arrived at independently. Tower keeps UNVERIFIED as a terminal state in an obligations ledger; CALC reports 10/10 correct with 2 unanswered rather than calling a provider outage a failure. Together they are the corpus's evidence that distinguishing absence of data from bad data is the recurring mark of a trustworthy agent.

value: The SNIIM scraper is the first thing to fail: an ASP.NET HTML page with no API, which already answers 503 to anything without browser headers, is a dependency the team cannot schedule with the publisher. The saved-response test detects a format change, but a wholesale price that is a day stale or silently missing produces a confident, wrong 'buy now' alert on the one channel where being late makes the alert worthless.

Two sources of truth for the same number nearly shipped: the backend summed by line amount while the screen recomputed, so the same receipt was simultaneously balanced and not. Any path where a validation rule and a displayed total are computed separately - including in the three agents that read the books - will diverge again on the next store that prints an unusual layout.

The unattended agent loop has no user-visible failure state. 'Retries on failure, every run logged' is the design, and a Cloud Run Job that quietly stops firing costs the user an unnoticed warning before a purchase; the green column is checked by the authors, not by the person who needed the alert.

The alert vocabulary at 28 hand-corrected Spanish products is fragile in the specific way that loses trust with this audience: gender and agreement errors ('papa esta mas barato') read as an outsider writing about your market. The fix they found - an article on every product plus verbs that carry no gender - does not scale on its own to the 222 published products and the meat, grain and oil sections they want to add next.

Cost scales with attention, not with value: a 2,596-token system prompt on every call was their biggest line, so a cheap day of many small questions is the worst economic case. The proposed fixes (prompt caching, lower thinking budget) are not in yet, and the unit figures that would show whether they work are only checkable against the authors' own invoice.

what_it_does.value: Ask anything with numbers in it, in Spanish with typos and slang: 'cuanto es el 15% de 800 pesos', 'vendi 40 tacos a 25 y gaste 300 en carne, cuanto gane'. Photograph a receipt and every line is transcribed - discounts, coupons and per-weight items included - and the app refuses to save if the rows do not add up to the printed total. Ask which package is cheaper: 2 kg at $245 or 6.81 kg at $1,050, where the big one looks like the deal and is 26% more expensive per kilo. Five agents run on their own every day: one reads wholesale prices from the government's market system, one compares against your own purchase history, one closes the books at night. The alert arrives before the purchase, because 'an alert you read once you have already paid is worthless'. Voice and camera input on a mobile-first PWA.

what_it_is.value: A money copilot for cash commerce that leaves no paper trail, in the Spanish people actually speak: the model turns a sentence into an expression and code evaluates it, a receipt that does not balance cannot be saved, and five scheduled agents warn you before you buy.

value: Make 'the model never does arithmetic' the architectural decision rather than a mitigation: the model turns language into a structured expression and code evaluates it, with the stated reason that money does not tolerate a plausible answer. Any product that lets a model produce the number it then acts on can be reduced to this sentence.

Refuse to persist money you cannot verify - a receipt whose rows do not sum to the printed total cannot be saved - and then read the rest of their story: the same rule left a user stuck with a disabled button and no way out, so pair the refusal with an explicit escape hatch before copying it.

Publish the bound, not the score: '0 errors in 30 cases; 95% upper bound on the error rate is about 10%' costs one sentence and is why a technical reader believes the other thirty. It also happens to be arithmetic a reader can check.

Teach your eval to tell wrong from blind. Reporting 10/10 with 2 unanswered on a provider-overload day instead of raising a false alarm is the difference between a monitor and an alarm; most agent scorecards conflate the two.

Log the thing that refutes you. finishReason logging was added to confirm a MAX_TOKENS hypothesis and instead proved it wrong (STOP, deterministically at temperature 0) - 'instrument before you diagnose' is the cheapest engineering culture in this corpus.
Pin a real saved response as a test against any scraped page you depend on, so you find out the day the publisher changes the format rather than the day your users do.
Say nothing most days: an agent that speaks every day gets ignored within a week, so the correct output is often empty. This is the opposite default of every 'proactive assistant' in the corpus.

Look for the category the data excludes by construction, not the workflow a model can now do: fiscal-receipt-fed price systems are excellent in Brazil and Argentina precisely because informal sellers are not in the receipts, and that is a market argument a wrapper cannot copy.

value.estimate: 5-7 weeks for a single-jurisdiction version a buyer would trust; a year of data work for the catalog that makes it worth using
value.why: The application is ordinary: photo preprocessing with Sharp, a queue on Inngest, Prisma over Postgres, Next.js and Stripe, and a multimodal model call with search grounding for part numbers and live prices - two or three weeks for someone fluent in that stack. The time goes into the parts catalog and the pricing source, which are the only defensible parts of the product and are not built here at all: structuring OEM data per make, model and year, keeping prices from becoming stale, and deciding what to return when coverage is thin. Adding a second jurisdiction (ECE instead of DOT/SAE, EUR, per-country import and inspection rules) is a further multiplier rather than a config flag. A clone can reproduce the flow quickly; it cannot reproduce the asset.

data_and_models.value: Two vendor capabilities and one internal asset: Gemini 2.5 Flash, Pro and Flash-Lite via @google/genai for the multimodal read (with automatic failover between the three), Google Search grounding for OEM part-number lookup and live price verification, and a proprietary parts catalog the page sizes at 700,000-plus records across 60-plus makes. Prisma plus PostgreSQL hold estimates and users, Inngest runs the pipeline, R2 or Supabase hold images, Sharp normalises them before inference. No model is trained, and no accuracy, precision or price-error figure is published for either the vision step or the grounding step - the numbers on the page are throughput (under 2 minutes), asset size (700,000 records, 60-plus makes) and band edges (40 and 70 percent), not measurement.

how_it_works.value: Next.js App Router with TypeScript, Tailwind and React on the front; Prisma over PostgreSQL (Neon) for state, Cloudflare R2 or Supabase for media, Sharp for image preparation, and Inngest for the asynchronous estimate pipeline. Stripe carries multi-currency billing. Recognition and pricing run on Gemini 2.5 Flash, Pro and Flash-Lite through @google/genai, with automatic failover between the three models, and Google Search grounding is used to look up OEM part numbers and verify live prices. Nothing is trained; the parts catalog the page calls proprietary, at 700,000-plus records across 60-plus vehicle makes, is presented as an asset rather than as something built here, and its construction is not documented.

how_they_tested.value: No evaluation of any kind is described: no precision or recall on part identification, no back-test of repair estimates against shop invoices or auction outcomes, no error bars on the Loss Ratio, no hold-out by make or model year, and no mention of a test suite. The only quantitative structure on the page is the Loss Ratio band policy - Low under 40 percent, Moderate 40 to 70, High above 70 - which is a threshold choice presented as matching 'EU & US salvage threshold standards' with no citation for either standard. The honesty device the page does describe is in the interface rather than in a benchmark: scarcity detection and advisory banners that flag where the catalog does not reach.

limits_they_disclosed.value: Coverage is the stated problem, and the page treats it as a design constraint rather than an edge case: it describes scarcity detection and advisory banners whose job is to communicate the limits of the parts catalog honestly instead of returning empty or misleading results, with the operating principle stated plainly - a wrong OEM code shown with false confidence is worse than showing no result. The second named difficulty is jurisdiction: two standards bodies, two currencies, and per-country import, title, emissions and inspection rules that have to be attached to the right estimate rather than translated after the fact, which is also what pulls Stripe multi-currency into the stack.

value.relation: both turn a stream of sensor evidence into a regulatory-flavoured verdict for a human to act on, and neither page publishes an accuracy figure - the fisheries tool goes further and states there is no ground truth for its risk classification, while Carbender's page implies its bands come from external standards without naming them. Read together, they are the two failure modes of the same design: admit the measurement problem, or borrow authority from a regulator.

both end in an artifact a person checks rather than an action the system takes - a repair plan PDF against a cited diff - and both leave the accuracy of the underlying judgement unmeasured. The difference is what they attach evidence to: Continuity grounds a claim against the live web and shows the citation next to the verdict, while Carbender grounds a part number against a proprietary catalog the reader cannot inspect, so its traceability stops at the vendor boundary.

both put a machine-readable judgement in front of a purchase decision and both monetise through the transaction surface rather than the model; the marketplace tool's advantage is that its output is checked by the market on the next listing, whereas a repair estimate is only checked when the parts arrive, so the feedback loop is months long.

what_breaks_first.value: Catalog coverage, on both ends of the pipeline. The 700,000-row figure is spread over 60-plus makes and their model years, so the first user with a twelve-year-old European hatchback gets either no parts or a plausible wrong code - and the scarcity banner only helps if scarcity is detected against coverage the product actually measures rather than against a lookup that happens to miss. Second, the severity-to-cost link: the bands assume the repair estimate is close enough to divide by resale value, and near 40 and 70 percent a modest error in labour or parts changes 'repairable' into 'Total Loss' with no stated error model to tell the buyer which side of the line they are on. Third, spatial normalisation: the driver-side versus passenger-side disambiguation is the difference between quoting a mirror or a fender, and a cropped, low-light auction photo is precisely where a 3D-normalisation step degrades.

what_it_does.value: Photos go in and a structured estimate comes out: damaged parts identified against an OEM catalog, each graded Severe, Moderate or Cosmetic, with 3D spatial normalisation used to tell driver-side from passenger-side damage rather than trusting the photo's left and right. Every identified part carries a real-market price report, and the parts assemble into a Repair Planner that exports a PDF. A Loss Ratio - Total Estimated Repair Cost divided by Clean Market Resale Value - is banded Low under 40 percent, Moderate 40 to 70, High above 70, described as matching EU and US salvage threshold standards, and a High ratio returns a Total Loss verdict. Jurisdiction changes the vocabulary (US DOT/SAE standards and USD, EU ECE in EUR) and adds country-aware import, title, emissions and inspection warnings. A separate free tool at carbender.com/window-sticker turns a VIN into a Monroney window sticker, and the whole product is a zero-download mobile web app in four locales (English, Lithuanian, Polish and US English).

what_it_is.value: A salvage-buyer's tool that turns damage photos into a priced OEM parts list, grades severity panel by panel, and divides the repair estimate by clean resale value to say whether the car is worth fixing at all - with US and EU rulebooks treated as different products, and missing parts coverage announced instead of papered over.

what_to_steal.value: Publish the decision rule, not just the score: the Loss Ratio names both inputs, states the band edges, and returns a verdict - a reader can recompute it and argue with it, which is more than most 'AI estimate' products offer. Then steal the failure-surface design: scarcity detection wired to an advisory banner, with the explicit principle that admitting no coverage beats a confident wrong answer. Region should be an input, not a translation - standards family, currency and title/import/emissions/inspection rules change what the estimate means, so carry them through the model call and the UI together. Free adjacent utility as acquisition: a VIN-to-window-sticker generator that costs nothing to run and lands the same audience on the paid product. And three model tiers with automatic failover in a flow running against an auction clock.

hazard.note: This is a money decision dressed in regulatory vocabulary. The product returns a Total Loss verdict and a repair estimate that a buyer may bid against, while invoking DOT, SAE and ECE standards, country-specific import, title, emissions and inspection requirements, and a Loss Ratio band policy described as 'matching EU & US salvage threshold standards' with no citation and no named issuing body for either threshold. Nothing on the page states who is liable when the estimate is wrong, no accuracy figure exists for either the part identification or the price, and the resale denominator comes from another estimate rather than a transaction record, so a High-band verdict near a boundary can flip on inputs that are both soft. The team's stated posture is the right instinct - a wrong OEM code shown with false confidence is worse than no result - but an interface banner is not a compliance sign-off, and a tool that names regulators should either cite them or stop invoking them. Held from promotion on that basis: publishable as a documented case, not as a usable figure.

value.why: The infrastructure they describe is standard GCP work and their two structural tricks are small to implement once you know them. What cannot be hurried is authoring and maintaining rule text for the jurisdictions you serve, plus someone qualified to confirm each rule still matches the regulation.

data_and_models.value: No model training. Two Gemini calls - fact extraction, then reasoning against hand-written versioned YAML rulesets - with citation mandatory in the output schema and prompt plus model version recorded per check. The regulated content is the rulesets themselves, authored by the team; nothing on the page says who reviewed them against the current text of the regulations they cite.

how_it_works.value: Five containerised services on Cloud Run behind one FastAPI gateway, declared in Terraform, running in a real GCP project with no emulators. Ingestion and compliance agents are Cloud Tasks workers (OIDC between them); state lives in Firestore, the audit trail in append-only BigQuery, documents and reports in Cloud Storage; a Cloud Scheduler job triggers Cloud Workflows for the weekly report. React dashboard with Firebase Auth on the front. Two decisions carry the design: tenant identity is taken only from verified JWT claims, never from a body or query parameter, so no code path can read across tenants; and rewriting an audit row needs both bigquery.tables.updateData and bigquery.jobs.create, so the writer identity holds the first and is denied the second - UPDATE and DELETE are unavailable to their own application rather than merely unused by it.

how_they_tested.value: Pytest is declared in Built With and 536 tests are reported, including a named concurrency case, but no repository, CI run or test output is linked, so the count and the coverage are the team's assertion. No accuracy figure is claimed for the compliance verdicts themselves - no eval set of documents with known-correct outcomes, no false-positive or missed-finding rate against an auditor's judgement.

limits_they_disclosed.value: Prompting does not stop fabrication, so rules live in versioned YAML, a citation is mandatory in the output contract, prompt and model version are recorded against every check so a verdict can be reproduced, and when the model cannot ground a verdict it escalates instead of guessing. Their weekly report workflow existed, was scheduled and looked healthy in the console for three weeks without ever running: Cloud Scheduler was being refused with PERMISSION_DENIED into a log nobody read, and fixing it uncovered six defects behind each other (missing invoker role, doubled URL scheme, a request to a route the service does not serve, a hardcoded tenant list, a service account without Firestore access, a missing log-writer permission). They conclude the actual bug was that nothing was watching; there are now uptime checks and alerts on scheduler and workflow failures. Terraform silently dropped a hand-set environment variable because Cloud Run replaces its env list wholesale, which cost every platform admin console access at once; the same trap sat in payment flags where a default of false would have quietly removed PayPal credentials on a fresh checkout, so those variables are now required and a missing value stops the deploy. An unregistered domestic Razorpay account rejects international cards even in live mode, and Stripe's INR conversion fee turned a $50 audit into a much larger rupee figure at checkout, so they removed Stripe and use PayPal for international customers.

what_breaks_first.value: The rulesets. Eighty-eight hand-authored YAML rules against regulations that amend without notice, with their own roadmap conceding that change detection is not built yet - so the first failure mode is a document auto-approved against a superseded rule, reported with a citation that still resolves to a real but obsolete clause. Second: the escalation threshold, since auto-approve on 'routine' documents is only as safe as the classifier that calls a document routine.

what_it_does.value: Upload a document (PDF, text, CSV or image). An ingestion agent extracts the facts with Gemini; a compliance agent reasons over them against the ruleset for that industry and jurisdiction and returns a risk score where every verdict carries its citation. Routine documents auto-approve, edge cases escalate to a human reviewer with the reasoning attached, every decision is appended to an immutable audit trail, and a scheduled workflow produces weekly reports with a Gemini executive summary. Currently 16 rulesets, 88 rules, 12 jurisdiction profiles: NDIS and aged care in Australia, corporate compliance in India, and GDPR, CCPA, PIPEDA, LGPD, PDPA and POPIA.

what_it_is.value: Document compliance checks where every verdict must cite a rule in a versioned ruleset, with an append-only audit trail the writing identity cannot rewrite.

what_to_steal.value: Grant the writer identity the append permission and deny it the job-starting permission, so history cannot be rewritten by the application that writes it; derive tenant identity only from verified token claims so there is no request field to tamper with; record prompt and model version against every generated verdict so a decision can be reproduced months later; make environment variables required rather than defaulted, because a permissive default on a fresh checkout silently removed credentials.

value.relation: the same shape — a machine ranking facts for a human to act on, deliberately stopping short of acting — and the two pages differ almost entirely on whether the judgement is checkable: Continuity returns old text, new text, a citation and a confidence score per claim, while the fisheries tool returns a risk classification whose own page says there is no ground truth for it.

both convert an unverifiable judgement into an artifact a person can check (a cited diff, a signed finding) and both keep the human as the writer of record; the difference is what they attach evidence to — one grounds a claim against the live web on a schedule, the other against a versioned rule set in CI.

both are staged agent pipelines that publish a dollar figure, and read together they move the number worth tracking: Greenlight quotes cost per run against a measured output, Continuity quotes total build cost and explains that fixtures made every later iteration free — so iteration cost, not run cost, is what decides whether a pipeline is developable.

what_breaks_first.value: The fixed staleness window. 'Skip what was verified last week' is a single guess about decay rates applied uniformly, and it is wrong in both directions for the facts this targets: a film's release date almost never moves, while 'current holder of X' can move in a day — so the budget is spent re-checking stable facts while the volatile ones age out between passes. Second: the reviewer's queue. 'Sources disagree' is a terminal category with no triage described, and on a long contested article it can hold a large share of the claims; a maintainer handed forty cited diffs and thirty unresolved disagreements has been given a new job, not a lighter one.

what_it_does.value: One button on an article page; no setup, config or schedule to configure. The agent reads the page, writes down every factual claim it makes one at a time, decides which are worth checking now (claims verified last week are skipped), researches each on the live web through Parallel, judges what came back with Gemini as still-true, changed or sources-disagree, drafts the edit with the citation attached, cross-checks that edit against the rest of the page so one fixed paragraph cannot contradict another, and hands it back as a diff with old text, new text, sources and a confidence score. Then it stops and waits: approve, rewrite or throw out — nothing reaches the page until a person says so.

what_it_is.value: A MediaWiki companion that re-reads a page fact by fact on a schedule, researches each claim against the live web, and hands the maintainer a cited diff for every fact that quietly stopped being true — never writing to the article itself.

what_to_steal.value: Record fixtures on the first live run — write every search result and model response to disk once, and every later iteration is free; that single habit is what made the whole thing developable on a hackathon budget. Keep vendor SDKs at the edges around a dependency-free core so the interesting logic runs on a bare interpreter with no key. Schedule re-verification per claim with a last-checked and next-due time rather than per page, and keep a link graph between claims so an edit to one paragraph can be checked against its neighbours. And always hand back a diff with citations instead of writing to the system of record.

value.why: The demonstrated build is a two-person MERN app with a structured questionnaire, three reasoning loops over MongoDB, Twilio and Gmail send, a Calendar booking call and a KPI dashboard, which is weeks, not months. The expensive part is what the page does not show: a HIPAA posture - BAA with the model and messaging providers, consent to be messaged by an automated system, access control on the interaction logs - and the Dentrix/Eaglesoft integration every real clinic will ask for on day one, which is a licensing and connector problem rather than a coding one. Copy the audit-as-product and the approval gate in a weekend; ship this to paying clinics in a quarter.

data_and_models.value: Clinic profiles, patient interaction logs and KPI snapshots in MongoDB; patient history is passed into a structured Gemini prompt to write each reactivation message, so identifiable clinical and appointment history leaves the product on every agent turn. Inbound sources are the clinic's own systems through the audit questionnaire plus Google Calendar, Google My Business and Twilio/Gmail; the message channels are SMS and email. No model is trained or fine-tuned. Nothing on the page addresses HIPAA, a business associate agreement with the model or messaging providers, patient consent to be messaged by an automated system, de-identification before the prompt, encryption at rest, or who can read the interaction logs - and the stated expansion is into medical clinics, optometry and physiotherapy, i.e. the same patient-data surface with more of it.

how_it_works.value: React, Vite and TypeScript for the dashboard, onboarding flow and agent activity feed; Node.js and Express for the REST API, agent orchestration and webhook handling; MongoDB for clinic profiles, patient interaction logs and KPI snapshots. Gemini via the Google AI Studio API powers the audit analysis, the agent reasoning, message generation and KPI interpretation. Twilio for SMS, the Gmail API for email campaigns, the Google Calendar and My Business APIs for the booking and inquiry loops. Backend in a container on Cloud Run, frontend on Firebase Hosting - a MERN stack with Google's AI layer on top, built by a two-person team. Each agent is a reasoning loop over a query: the Recall Agent pulls patients inactive 180+ days from MongoDB, passes the patient history to Gemini with a structured prompt, generates the message, sends it via Twilio and logs the interaction; a reply is handled by the same loop and booked through Google Calendar.

how_they_tested.value: No test suite, evaluation set, harness or run link is published anywhere on the page. The quality work is described only as prompt engineering plus a staff feedback loop in which clinic users rated and adjusted message quality during early use. The one figure offered as evidence of operation is '84 agent actions executed in production (logged and verifiable)', which is a count of actions taken rather than of outcomes measured, and it is the number that contradicts the growth claim in the same section. There is no repository to look for tests in.

limits_they_disclosed.value: Four difficulties, three of them about the data and one about trust. Dental data is messy - Dentrix, Eaglesoft, plain Excel - and building an intake flexible enough to normalise it without deep integrations was harder than expected, answered by the structured audit questionnaire that extracts what is needed from any source system. Agent reliability and tone: patient-facing messages had to sound clinic-branded rather than chatbot-generic, which took significant prompt engineering plus a feedback loop where clinic staff rated and adjusted message quality early. Meaningful KPIs versus vanity metrics: the first dashboard tracked around 40 measures, dentists had no time to interpret them, so it was stripped to twelve with a sentence of interpretation under each ('your no-show rate is 18%. industry average is 10%. fixing this could recover approximately $X per month'). And the biggest obstacle was not the product but permission - convincing owners to let agents message their patients - solved with the approval-first mode for the first two weeks.

value.relation: the same buyer, the same lesson arrived at from the other side. AttainDesk is an SMB support desk whose conclusion after a year of real use was 'less AI, not more'; DentOps is an SMB operations layer that reached 'AI-native doesn't mean AI-everywhere' from 15 clinics and a two-week approval gate. Both independently shrink the model's authority in front of small business owners, and neither has a public artefact to verify the results with.

a study in how to handle a money number. Both products put a dollar figure in front of a cash-poor owner - '47 lapsed patients worth about $14,000' against CALC's per-kilo and per-receipt arithmetic. CALC's figures re-derive and are published with their denominators; DentOps' headline is an average over an unstated denominator and contradicts its own log. The pair is the corpus's clearest illustration that a dollarized claim is a claim, not a style.

identical trust architecture, opposite disclosure. Both gate an autonomous agent behind a verification step before it acts on the world - a passing test suite there, a human approval window here - and both then publish a headline speed or volume figure with no denominator. DentOps at least supplies a production log to be contradicted by.

both automate outreach to people in a clinical context, and both have to decide how much of the patient the model may see. Medvoice narrows the channel deliberately - a photo and a spoken instruction, nothing that reads like a record - while DentOps puts patient history in the prompt to personalise a text message.

value: The headline metric, in front of a buyer. If 330 is patients *surfaced by a query* rather than patients rebooked, then the recall rate the product is judged on is a search result count, and the dashboard's 'reappointment rate' column is the number that will disagree with the sales deck - which is exactly the disagreement already visible between the 330 and the 84 logged actions.

The un-messaged boundary: patient history is in the prompt for every outbound message. The first security or compliance conversation with a real clinic - or the first practice-management vendor that reads the integration as a data-processing relationship - requires an answer the page does not contain: no BAA, no consent model for automated messages to patients, no de-identification, no statement of who can read the interaction logs. The expansion to medical, optometry and physiotherapy makes the same gap wider rather than narrower.

The intake. Everything after the audit depends on data that came from a questionnaire and a spreadsheet snapshot; the waitlist backfill, the 180-day window and the reappointment tracking all go stale the moment the clinic books in Dentrix and not in Google Calendar. Until the native connectors exist, the agents are reasoning over a copy, and a stale copy sends a reminder for an appointment that was already moved.

Tone, at scale and per clinic: they got 'warm, clinic-branded, not chatbot' by hand with a staff rating loop on a handful of clinics. That is a prompt-and-review process, not a guarantee, and the failure mode is a message that reads wrong to a patient - the one error class a clinic will not forgive, because it is sent under the dentist's name.

The single-number pricing: $249 per month with Twilio SMS, Gmail sending and Gemini inference on every turn. At 330 conversations per clinic per month the variable cost is not small, and the page gives no margin figure - so the growth claim and the price only survive together if the real volume is the one the 84 actions suggest.

what_it_does.value: Onboarding is a 20-minute structured audit of the clinic's operations with existing tools connected - Google Calendar, the practice management system, or a spreadsheet if there is nothing better. Gemini analyses the answers and returns a prioritised ops gap report that says where revenue is leaking and estimates the dollar impact of each gap, rendered as a visual priority matrix. From that report the clinic gets a tailored agent team: a Recall Agent that finds patients inactive for 180+ days and sends personalised reactivation messages over SMS and email, tracking reappointment rate weekly; a No-Show Agent that runs confirmation sequences at 48 hours and 2 hours out and backfills cancelled slots from the waitlist; a New Patient Agent that answers Google My Business inquiries, follows up missed calls and requests reviews after the appointment. The dashboard carries twelve KPIs in three departments - patient ops (recall, no-show, reappointment, chair utilisation), revenue (per visit, treatment acceptance, average invoice, monthly trend) and marketing (acquisition by source, cost per new patient, review count and rating) - updated daily, with plain-English interpretation under each number. Every agent action is logged to an activity feed, and in the first two weeks nothing goes out unreviewed: the clinic approves each message before it is sent.

what_it_is.value: An AI operations layer for a two-chair dental practice: a 20-minute audit prices the leaks, a small agent team sends recall and no-show messages behind a two-week approval gate, and twelve KPIs on one dashboard explain themselves in plain English.

value: Sell the diagnosis before the automation: a 20-minute structured audit that returns a prioritised gap report with a dollar estimate attached to each gap. They expected it to be a funnel step and found it was the artefact customers shared with a business partner - a paid-shaped deliverable that also happens to be the onboarding. Works for any agent product whose buyer cannot articulate their own leak.

Approval-first autonomy with a stated clock: for the first two weeks every agent message is reviewed by the clinic before it goes out, then it goes automatically. This is the trust ramp the rest of the corpus argues about in the abstract, priced in days and applied to the highest-stakes channel (their patients).

Cap the dashboard and interpret every cell: cut from ~40 measures to 12 that map to money, and put the sentence under the number ('your no-show rate is 18%. industry average is 10%. fixing this could recover approximately $X per month'). The comparison plus the dollar is the whole feature - a KPI without a benchmark is decoration.

Niche the vertical before the workflow: the reason the recall agent is credible is that '180+ days inactive', '6+ months', 'chair utilisation' and 'treatment acceptance rate' are dental-specific objects. The same loop over a generic 'small business' has nothing to reason with.

Use the prospect's own numbers as the close. '47 lapsed patients worth about $14,000' converted in one call every time, because the arithmetic came out of their data - and note the discipline implied: the estimate is only persuasive because it is specific enough to be checked.

hazard.note: Regulated-outcome language was stamped by the engine's own test, so it is answered here rather than argued away. What the team said about the regulated part of this product is: nothing. The page states that patient history is passed into the model on every agent turn, that patient interaction logs live in MongoDB, that messages go to patients over Twilio SMS and Gmail, and that the expansion plan runs through medical clinics, optometry and physiotherapy - and it contains no mention of HIPAA, a business associate agreement with the model provider or Twilio, consent to be contacted by an automated system, de-identification before the prompt, retention limits on the logs, or who inside a clinic may read them. The one control the page does describe, the two-week approval-first window, governs *tone* - whether a message should be sent - and not data, so it is not an answer to this hazard. `team_disclaimed: false` is therefore correct and the record is held for a second reason beyond its arithmetic: a builder copying the operations model should copy the audit-as-product and the approval gate, and must not assume the compliance surface was thought about. The strongest available reading is that the hazard is unaddressed rather than mishandled - a hackathon page is not a data-processing agreement - which is why it is written here as an open obligation and not as misconduct.

value.estimate: multi-week
value.why: the app itself is a fortnight of competent work — a Laravel API with Sanctum, MySQL, multi-currency ledger arithmetic, six integrations and a scheduler — but the parts that make it feel finished are the ones nobody budgets for: locale-aware currency formatting, Lottie-driven progression art, and per-feed degradation policies. An agent team with a component library and no art pipeline lands the ledger and misses the house.

data_and_models.value: No model and no training data: the app is deterministic arithmetic over live third-party reference data, with the gamification layer a progression table rather than a predictor. The design question it has to get right is staleness — every converted balance, loan quote and simulated return is only as current as the last scheduler run — and the page documents the refresh cadences but publishes no freshness indicator, no last-updated stamp in the UI description, and no fallback for when a feed is down.

how_it_works.value: Flutter 3.35.3 on Dart 3.9.2 with Provider for state, fl_chart for charts, flutter_svg for vectors and Lottie for the house animations. Laravel Framework 9.52.20 serves the API with Sanctum tokens for authentication, MySQL for persistence, form Request validation, timezone handling from UTC to local, and Jobs plus artisan Commands to refresh external data. Six external feeds are wired in: OpenExchangeRates for live FX rates and the currency base table; Banco Central de la República Argentina's DataAPI for the official rates that back the loan and plazo-fijo simulators; CoinGecko for crypto prices and price history used by the digital-investment simulator; TwelveData for equities and bond data feeding the same simulation model; the World Bank PPP API for purchasing-power parity, which drives Casa Finova's visuals and cross-country purchasing-power comparison; and Brevo SMTP for password-recovery mail delivered through a native deep link. Refresh is a Laravel Scheduler split into three cadences — daily for BCRA indicators and official rates, frequent for CoinGecko prices and OpenExchangeRates, weekly for slow-moving macroeconomic data such as World Bank PPP. Password reset uses a native deep link, tokens are kept server-side, and avatars are generated or custom.

what_breaks_first.value: The rate path. Every balance, simulator and report depends on a converted value, and the only thing keeping it current is a scheduler the page describes without a freshness guard: no 'rates last updated' stamp, no described behaviour when OpenExchangeRates or BCRA is unreachable. A missed run therefore does not error — it quietly mis-values the whole app, and the number a user acts on looks exactly like the number that was correct. Second is the deep-link reset: a native deep link is one of the few auth surfaces where a mis-registered URL scheme or an Android App Link / iOS Universal Link mismatch turns password recovery into a dead end, and nothing on the page says how that was verified.

what_it_does.value: Finova is a mobile money manager (Flutter front end, Laravel REST backend) built around three interlocking loops: record, convert, and be rewarded. Money lives in typed sources — wallets, bank accounts, cash, cards — each holding its own balance in its own currency, and the app shows that balance converted into the user's base currency in real time. Income and expense entries are made fast, and an entry in a currency other than the source's is converted automatically; the ledger is then filterable by category, date, type, source and free-text search, grouped by day with running totals. Goals are amounts you aim at, and linking a goal to a source turns on automatic reserve, with progress drawn live. The gamification layer generates periodic financial objectives that behave like missions: completing one awards XP, XP accumulates into levels, and levels unlock visual elements and upgrades in “Casa Finova”, a house that is a rendering of your financial state — it evolves with your progress, its sky moves through day, sunset and night, and its changes animate in Lottie. Statistics are monthly totals, income versus expense, per-category distribution and a global converted balance, charted with fl_chart. On top of the ledger sit simulators — loans driven by official central-bank rates, traditional fixed-term investments (plazo fijo) and digital ones (crypto) — plus a currency converter covering more than 160 currencies with locale-aware formatting, and exportable custom reports.

what_it_is.value: A Spanish-language personal-finance app where saving is a game: multi-currency ledgers priced off six live external feeds, and a house whose skies and rooms change as your balance improves.

what_to_steal.value: Source the difficulty from outside the product. Casa Finova's progression is driven by live external state — PPP from the World Bank, official rates from the central bank — so the game layer inherits a world the user cannot farm by doing nothing. For any agent that has to prove something rather than appear helpful, that is the move worth copying: bind rewards or verdicts to data the operator does not control, and the loop stops being self-flattering. Second, cheap: convert on write, not on read. Storing each entry in its own currency and resolving the base-currency value when the record is created makes a stale rate table an immutability problem instead of a silently-rewritten ledger.

what_it_does.value: User drops a screenplay. The system reads it whole, splits it into chapters, breaks chapters into shots, casts characters, writes prompts, generates footage, then inspects what it made: if shot 3 contains a person who should not be there it notices and folds that into the retry instruction. The user presses keep or again. Before any spend it quotes odds: this chapter is 12 shots, ~$4.50, about half will pass first try. Casting is a hard gate; a character reference costs $0.02 while a shot costs $1 and a finished segment ~$20, so every decision is pushed down the cost ladder. Face is an input, look is an output: an uploaded photo is locked as identity while only the style re-renders, and wardrobe is per chapter. Style buttons carry their own success adjustment (photorealistic −10pt vs animation +12/+15pt). Every generation and every keep/again verdict is written to ClickHouse, so once enough similar shots exist the estimate switches from built-in priors to that user's own numbers and says which one you are looking at plus the sample size. After casting, every prompt is exportable.

what_it_is.value: Drop a screenplay; nine agents read it, cast it, price it, shoot it, and watch what they made — with the quote shown before you press the button.

what_to_steal.value: Two moves, and they compose: (1) quote the cost and the pass rate before the button, and push every hesitation down the price ladder (settle a character at $0.02, not $1); (2) log every verdict row into a store you can query, then let the estimate switch from your priors to the user's own measured numbers and label which one they are reading, with sample size. On-device speech recognition on a late-night mumble, then a six-label pass over two minutes of prose: sarcasm, a flat 'I'm fine', a day that was actually bad but got narrated cheerfully all produce a confident label with no uncertainty attached, and the calendar of faces becomes a record of what the model guessed. Because nothing in the UI can tell a wrong label from an unusual day, the failure mode is invisible to exactly the user the product is for.

The VIP voice-level signal is the one place audio-derived features leave the device, and the page does not say whether the baseline it is compared against is computed on device or on the server. If it is server-side, the 'recordings stay on your phone' sentence needs a qualifier a reader can find - for a product whose pitch is privacy, an ambiguous data boundary is a product bug.

The Sunday letter is the second thing to decay: a generated recap of six labels and a handful of day-titles reads warmly for two weeks and templated by week four, and there is no evaluation or user feedback anywhere on the page about whether anyone keeps opening it.

RevenueCat entitlements are the boring break: the trial, the three gates and the crown all depend on entitlement state being correct across reinstall and store-side refunds, and a gate that misfires in a journal the user cannot re-read is worse than a paywall. There is no test or CI evidence for the billing path, which is the path that carries money.

what_it_does.value: Tap the mic and talk for up to two minutes, or type on days you cannot speak out loud. On-device speech recognition turns the audio into text; the model returns six feeling labels (joy, bashfulness, surprise, sadness, anger, tiredness), a short title for the day and one gentle line from the companion. Those labels become physical objects: little characters, one colour per feeling, that drop into that day's box, roll when you tilt the phone, squish when tapped, and fall back in when flung off the screen. A calendar of faces holds every day's words, feelings and your own voice if you kept it, with look-backs over a week, a month or a year, and every Sunday night the companion writes a letter about the week. Four limits are authored as a section of their own: no diagnosis, no advice, no pushy encouragement - 'the AI is instructed to receive, not to fix'; no streak guilt, since a current streak shows only while it lasts, '0 days' and 'streak lost' are never displayed and totals only go up; not a medical device, stated in the app, the store listing and the terms, with signposting to professional help when things feel heavy; and recordings stay on the phone, with only the transcript sent for the reading plus, for VIP, coarse voice-level signals compared against the user's own baseline, and AI can be switched off entirely.

what_it_is.value: Voice journaling that reads six feelings instead of asking for a score: recordings stay on the phone, the model is instructed to receive rather than fix, and the paywall only appears at the moment someone reaches for more.

value: Put the paywall at the moment of reaching and nowhere else: three named triggers, each reached by someone already asking for more, each keeping what they made before the prompt appears (talk twice in a day and your words are stored first; tap 1mo/3mo/1y and you see the week you can already see; tap an empty day and you are invited to fill it). Feature screens carry no locks and no 'you have run out' state at all, only a small crown on the ranges beyond the free window. This is a monetisation rule that costs nothing to adopt and is the opposite of the metered-gate default.

Design the retention mechanic so it cannot punish: a streak is shown only while it is alive, '0 days' and 'streak lost' never render, and totals only go up. In any product where the tracked object is a bad week, the counter is the harm.

State the model's job as a boundary in the product, not in a blog post: 'the AI is instructed to receive, not to fix', no advice, no diagnosis, and the non-medical-device claim made in the app, the store listing and the terms together, with signposting to professional help - plus a switch to turn the AI off entirely, which is the disclosure that makes the rest believable.

Make the derived signal tactile instead of charted: emotions become objects in a box you can tilt, tap and fling. A chart invites analysis; a physics toy invites return. Same data, different second use.

value.estimate: 6-9 weeks for the agent roster plus the schema surface; another quarter for the four media pipelines and the editorial tooling
value.why: The core loop is a fan-out with grounding: one event, N lens prompts each pinned to a region's outlets through search grounding, rendered side by side with tone labels - a few weeks in React, Express and Firestore, and the SPA-plus-Cloud-Run shape is well trodden. And the editorial layer - curating Common Ground, maintaining /corrections - is recurring human cost rather than build cost, which is why a clone of this is smaller than its feature list and bigger than its line count.

data_and_models.value: Gemini 3 Flash with Google Search grounding runs every lens, pointed at each region's own outlets; Gemini Native Audio renders the daily radio bulletin; Imagen 4 makes the topic imagery; Suno makes the per-topic songs; Firestore persists topics, perspectives and donor records, and Firebase Storage holds media. No model is trained and no retrieval configuration is published: the page states no per-region coverage figure, no rate at which a lens's sentences are unsupported by the cited source, and no fallback policy for when a region's press is unreachable - while naming that exact failure as the thing that turns multi-perspective AI into ventriloquism. The measured numbers on the page are about the surface (schema score, load time), not about the journalism.

how_it_works.value: React 19 with TypeScript and Vite as a client-side SPA, Express on Firebase App Hosting (Cloud Run underneath), Firestore for persistence and Firebase Storage for media, Imagen 4 for imagery and Gemini 3 Flash with Search grounding for the lens agents. The part the page spends most of its technical detail on is the machine-readable surface: every topic page ships a schema.org NewsArticle whose hasPart is an ItemList of Claim items, each with a per-perspective @id anchor and its own citation array, and the Jester carries a disambiguatingDescription marking it as satire so downstream models will not read it as fact. Alongside it: llms.txt and a 42,000-word llms-full.txt, ai-plugin.json, an OpenAPI 3.0.3 document, IndexNow pings, and a fully public no-auth /api/topics/recent endpoint.

how_they_tested.value: No evaluation of journalistic quality is described: no precision or recall against a labelled set of regional articles, no inter-rater check between lenses and human correspondents, no measurement of how often a perspective's claim is unsupported by its own citation, and no test-suite mention. The closest thing to a measurement on the page is an unnamed 'recent independent GEO audit' that scored schema 99/100 and Trustworthiness 82/100 - a machine-readability audit of metadata, not of content accuracy, with no auditor, date or rubric published. The one figure that does carry a before/after denominator is load time (30-45s to under 1s TTI), and the page volunteers a measured defect count in the same area: about ninety unresolved grounding redirect URLs per topic page.

limits_they_disclosed.value: The challenges section is a set of post-mortems rather than a list of feature difficulty. Firebase App Hosting silently ignored the hosting block in firebase.json, so sitemap and RSS returned 404 with no error anywhere, and the fix was explicit Express proxies in server.ts. Suno failed quietly: a null data payload produced an undefined taskId, JSON.stringify dropped the key, and the client polled /api/music/status/undefined fifty times against {code: 200, data: null}; it was fixed at three layers - a real 502 from the server, bailing after five consecutive nulls, and refusing to start on an empty, 'undefined' or 'null' id. And a Firestore rule written for /donations/{docId} did not match the client's /donors/{docId} path, which went unnoticed for months because the Admin SDK bypasses rules - so only the admin UI was broken, silently.

value.relation: both convert an unverifiable judgement into a machine-checkable artifact - a signed finding in a CI matrix against a Claim object with a citation array - and both leave the same gap: the artifact proves the format, not the accuracy of what is inside it. ACM measures its own detectors while Newspectives does not measure its lenses, which is the sharper omission given that the lens output is read as fact by other models.

both attach citations to language a model generated and both keep a human as the writer of record, but they differ on direction and schedule: Continuity re-checks existing claims over time and hands back a diff, Newspectives generates fresh accounts of one event across regions and hands back a comparison. Neither publishes a false-negative rate, and in both cases that rate is what the user is actually buying.

both sit in the sector where the hazard question is sign-off and both answer it with transparency rather than authority - methodology, editorial-standards and corrections pages against an audit-ready rule set. The pair is the catalog's clearest illustration that disclosure and compliance are different objects: one tells a reader how the output was made, the other tells an auditor what was checked.

what_breaks_first.value: The grounding fallback. When a region's outlets are unreachable - a paywall, a regional block, a story too new to have local coverage - the lens still produces fluent text, which is the exact failure the page names as ventriloquism, and there is no published policy for it and no rate for how often it happens. Second, citation integrity: about ninety redirect URLs per topic page still resolve through Vertex rather than to the publisher, so the citation array an agent inherits is a chain of third-party hops that can rot or 404 independently of the article. Third, the Jester: satire is marked with disambiguatingDescription, which most consumers ignore, so a joke line becomes a Claim in someone else's context window. Fourth, the Common Ground synthesis - labelled editorial curation on the site, but a downstream reader who takes the ItemList and drops the framing gets a machine-generated consensus view of a contested event, which is the one artifact this product's own principles say not to produce.

what_it_does.value: For a news event, roughly twenty configured regional lenses (about thirteen enabled by default - USA, China, Russia, India, Germany, UK, Israel, Arab World, Latin America, South Africa, a Humanitarian lens, a satirical 'Jester' and a Common Ground synthesis) each produce an account of the same story, grounded with Google Search against that region's press - BBC, Global Times, RT, Al Jazeera, NDTV, Times of Israel are the outlets named. The output is presented side by side with a tone classification and citations per perspective, and the Common Ground panel is an editor-curated synthesis rather than a model verdict. Three adjacent formats ride the same pipeline: a daily eight-minute AI radio bulletin on Gemini Native Audio, a per-topic Suno song, and a 20-second portrait video. Transparency pages are part of the product rather than a footer - /methodology, /editorial-standards and /corrections name the model and admit its limits.

what_it_is.value: A roster of about thirteen regional-lens agents reads one news event against each region's own press and publishes the frames side by side as schema.org Claim objects with citations - so the machines downstream inherit the framing, not just a flattened headline.

what_to_steal.value: Ship claim-level structured data rather than page-level: NewsArticle to hasPart to an ItemList of Claim objects, each perspective with its own @id anchor and citation array, so a consuming agent can attribute a sentence to a lens instead of to a URL. Use disambiguatingDescription to mark non-factual voices inside the same structure, and publish llms.txt, llms-full.txt, ai-plugin.json, an OpenAPI document, IndexNow pings and an unauthenticated read endpoint - treat machine readers as an audience and the transparency pages become distribution. Then take the operational post-mortems, the most reusable content on the page: never return a 200 with a null payload (make it a real 502), bail after five consecutive nulls instead of polling an 'undefined' id fifty times, refuse to start on an empty or 'undefined' config value, treat silently ignored hosting config as untrustworthy and proxy it explicitly, dismiss splash screens in about 150ms and load auth and settings in the background, and remember that Admin SDK paths bypass security rules, so rule-only tests prove nothing about an admin UI. Last: keep synthesis human and say so on the page.

how_it_works.value: Four agents under deterministic control flow. Intake reads the rulebook in two passes: pass one extracts obligation statements verbatim with no interpretation, pass two structures only what pass one found, so an invented requirement has nowhere to come from, and every requirement keeps the words it came from - which is what makes hallucination checkable 'in seconds'. Watch observes and nothing else: it makes zero model calls, mapping requirements to real tool surfaces (files in the live GitHub repo, public URLs, YouTube oEmbed, the Devpost project page) and reporting what it saw. Analyst decides what an observation means, with the state machine written as a pure function so a model never decides whether to escalate. Escalation is a policy table rather than a judgement: Kill requirements call immediately, Major wait until seven days out, Minor never call, and every call is idempotent because a thirty-minute schedule without that guard would phone about the same missing file repeatedly. Gemini is used in exactly two places - extracting the rulebook and writing the sentence a human hears - with the stated principle that control flow a model can talk itself out of is not control flow. how_they_tested.value: Two separate things, and the page is candid that they cover different ground. An eval: extraction scored against a hand-written ground-truth key of 29 obligations from the official rules, run three times, with recall, precision and F1 published for each run and the reason for each movement stated (a scorer bug, then four false credits found by auditing matched pairs by eye), plus 96% severity and 91% class agreement. A harness: 32 offline assertions over the state machine including both reversal paths, the escalation policy including idempotency, checker honesty and login-wall detection, running in about a second with no credentials. And one honest negative result that outweighs both: the harness was green for the entire period in which the login-wall defect existed, so thirty passing assertions proved the logic was correct and proved nothing about whether the logic could run on real input. No repository is linked, so neither suite can be read or re-run from here - the numbers are the author's, and only the F1 arithmetic is independently checkable.

limits_they_disclosed.value: Eight defects are listed, and the page's own reading is that they are the same bug wearing different hats: the system claiming knowledge it did not have. (1) Requirement IDs were unstable across extraction runs - the same obligation came back as `spinup-instructions-readme` one run and `spin-up-instructions` the next, and because the routing table keyed off those slugs, 9 of 12 requirements silently lost their tool surface and reported as unverifiable; routes now match on content, since content survives re-extraction and model-generated slugs do not. (2) Blank configuration read as failure - an unset URL reported UNMET rather than UNCHECKED, one tick from phoning the author at three in the morning about its own empty config file. (3) Expired credentials retried silently for five minutes and then died, which for a scheduled unattended agent is indistinguishable from a tick that found nothing wrong: silence meant both 'all clear' and 'I am broken'. (4) Conditional requirements were checked unconditionally - the rules say *if* the hosted site is private *then* supply credentials, Tower dropped the 'if' and the model invented the premise, narrating a private website that does not exist; declared facts now default to false so an unknown premise is never assumed true. (5) Narration was tied to state changes, so on the one tick where a call actually went out the requirement was already open, nothing changed, no sentence was generated, and Twilio read a raw Python fallback string down the phone line, list brackets included. (6) Tower apologised for a call it never made - it reversed a finding that had never been escalated and said 'please disregard our previous alert' when there had been none; call history is now an input to narration. (7) A dry run mutated state, resolving a pending finding and silently consuming it; dry runs are read-only. (8) The worst: Tower reported a requirement SATISFIED on the strength of words appearing on Devpost's login page - an unsubmitted draft redirects anonymous visitors to sign-in, that page returns HTTP 200, the status check believed it had fetched the project and pattern-matched against a login form; 'A 200 is not the same as reaching the thing you asked for.' The page then adds the finding that matters most for how to read the rest of it: the eval harness was green the entire time defect 8 existed, so thirty passing assertions proved the logic was correct and proved nothing about whether the logic could run on real input.

what_breaks_first.value: The requirement-to-tool-surface mapping. Every requirement needs a real place to look, and the failure mode the author hit first is a silent one: 9 of 12 requirements lost their route and reported as unverifiable. Anything the agent cannot reach - a private repo, an unlisted video, a platform page behind a login wall, a URL that returns 200 on a sign-in form - becomes a permanent UNVERIFIED, which is the correct answer and the one that makes the product look useless to a user who wants a green tick. Second is the severity policy: 'Kill calls immediately, Major waits until seven days out, Minor never calls' is tuned to one rulebook's shape, and a second competition with different disqualification clauses needs the table re-cut, not re-used. Third is the measured weakness they name themselves - extraction is structurally biased toward 'what must the entrant DO' over standing eligibility and legal clauses, and dedup folds adjacent legal text away - so the requirements most likely to cost you the prize are the ones the classifier is worst at.

what_it_does.value: Tower reads a competition rulebook once and turns it into a set of machine-checkable requirements, each carrying a severity and a specific place to look for evidence, then runs every thirty minutes for weeks, unattended, checking the live repository, public URLs and the video against that set. When something crosses the line it does not send an email: it calls the entrant's phone and says in one sentence what is about to disqualify them and how long they have. The part the author rates more highly is the reversal - when the problem is fixed, Tower calls back and stands its own alert down, and when it was wrong to call at all, it says so, because most verification agents only ever add findings. Three states carry that distinction and are explicitly not the same admission: RESOLVED (called, problem was real, fixed), RETRACTED (called, and the evidence was already in place - Tower was wrong), UNVERIFIED (could not actually check; 'Not satisfied. Not unmet. Unknown.'). The page names that third state as the spine of the system, with the reasoning that an agent which cannot distinguish 'everything is fine' from 'I could not see' is worse than no agent, because silence reads as an all clear.

what_it_is.value: A watchstander for competition rules: it extracts every obligation from a rulebook verbatim, gives each one a severity and a named place to look for evidence, re-checks the live repository, URLs and video every thirty minutes for weeks, and keeps RESOLVED, RETRACTED and UNVERIFIED as three different answers so that 'I could not see' can never read as an all clear.

what_to_steal.value: Make 'could not check' a value that propagates, not a gap that defaults to a verdict: UNVERIFIED is distinct from UNMET, blank config is distinct from failure, and an unknown premise in a conditional defaults to false rather than being narrated into existence. Then steal the two honesty mechanics that fall out of it - retraction as a first-class action (call back and stand down your own alert, and if you were wrong say RETRACTED, with call history as an input to narration so you cannot apologise for a call you never made), and routing by extracted content instead of model-generated identifiers, because slugs change between extraction runs and content does not.

how_it_works.value: Marketed as a longevity dashboard: it claims to translate clinical biomarker algorithms into an actionable score, “quantify, gamify, and actively reverse” aging. Built as React Native with NativeWind and Tailwind for the client, interactive 30-day, 90-day and one-year trend graphs. The core algorithm is the Levine PhenoAge model: nine biomarkers (albumin, creatinine, glucose, hs-CRP, lymphocyte percentage, mean corpuscular volume, red cell distribution width, alkaline phosphatase, white blood cell count) mapped to a mortality-risk score through a Gompertz distribution. Node.js services on Cloud Run with Firestore for documents and live sync.

Recomputing the model while drawing trend graphs pushed them to move the maths into lightweight on-device utility modules.

how_it_works.value: Three layers, per the page. An AI engine on Gemini 3.5 through the official google-genai SDK, used for code reasoning and patch generation. An agent framework on Google's ADK (Agent Development Kit) to sequence the multi-step reasoning and tool calls. Infrastructure on Google Cloud Run for serverless event handling and test execution, with Firestore holding audit logs and pipeline state. The declared tag list is wider than the prose — fastapi, firebase, gemini-api, google-cloud-firestore, google-genai, owasp, python, react, rest-api, tailwind-css, tanstack-router, typescript, vite — which reads as FastAPI at the webhook edge, a React/Vite/Tailwind console with TanStack Router, and OWASP as the reference frame for what counts as a finding rather than as a component.

shares the unattended-monitoring-plus-alerting loop over a live external surface, and stops one step earlier: VMS reports and a human acts, ZeroDay patches. The comparison is worth having because the extra automation step is where all of the difficulty lives (isolation, credentials, failure states) and it is the step this page describes least.

what_breaks_first.value: The detector, because it is undescribed. Everything downstream is careful — sandbox, tests, PR — but a patcher's ceiling is what it notices, and the page names two finding classes (SQL injection, exposed API keys) with no scanner, no ruleset and no false-negative story, so a miss is invisible by construction: the pipeline reports nothing and looks healthy. Second is the retry budget: "under 30 seconds" and "without causing infinite retry loops" cannot both be true for a hard patch, so on a real failure the run either times out mid-loop or silently gives up, and neither terminal state is published. Third is the trust surface — an agent with write access to repositories and a chat assistant over its own audit log is an approval target, and nothing on the page says who authorises the PR beyond a human clicking.

what_it_does.value: ZeroDay AI runs as a background agent over repositories. It watches for security flaws — the page names SQL injection and exposed API keys — and when one is detected it reads the surrounding code, writes a patch, executes the project's unit tests inside a containerized sandbox, and only then opens a GitHub pull request, with the run recorded as an audit log. The pipeline is described end to end as hands-off: a raw vulnerability webhook in, a tested pull request out. A chat assistant sits on top of the same state, and the screenshots show a live-scan view, a topology map of the monitored repositories and a Firestore-backed cloud-info panel. Nothing on the page claims it merges anything: the human review boundary is the pull request itself.

what_it_is.value: An agent that reads a security finding, writes the patch, runs the project's tests in a sandbox, and may not open the pull request until they pass.

what_to_steal.value: Make the verification step able to *refuse*: the agent's output is a pull request only after the target project's unit tests pass in a throwaway container, so "the model wrote something plausible" never becomes a state the system can reach. Then steal the honest framing of the loop around it — the page names the retry bound as the hard part instead of describing the loop as always converging, which is the sentence an autonomous-remediation design usually omits. Third, cheap and specific: a local pre-scan (Gemma, client-side, for syntax errors) before paying for a sandbox run is the same trick as checking a claim against a cache before calling the model — cost the cheap filter first, and only escalate what survives it.
